title: Claims, reasons and evidence
blurb: Take an argument apart: find the claim, the reasons, the evidence, the link between them, and the counterclaim with its rebuttal.
question: A letter to a hospital board says, 'Some board members argue the child care center would cost too much. However, St. Anne's found that savings on hiring more than covered its cost.' A TEAS item asks what role those two sentences play. Are they evidence, a reason, or something else?

teach.body: Formally, an argument is a claim (the author's position or thesis) supported by reasons and evidence, connected by a warrant (the reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim), and often answering a counterclaim with a rebuttal. In plain English: the claim is what the author wants you to believe, the reasons say why, the evidence proves the reasons, and the rebuttal deals with the other side.

(1) Pinecrest Hospital should offer free on-site child care for night-shift staff. (2) Nurses with young children struggle to find care after 7 p.m. (3) In a staff survey last spring, 41 percent of night nurses said child care was their main reason for thinking about leaving. (4) When St. Anne's Hospital opened a night child care center, its nurse turnover fell by a quarter within two years. (5) Keeping experienced nurses matters, because every nurse who leaves must be replaced and trained. (6) Some board members argue the center would cost too much. (7) However, St. Anne's found that its savings on hiring more than covered the center's cost.

children.label: Reason (2)
children.sub: Night care is hard to find

head: Type
What it looks like
Pinecrest example
teach.caption: Anecdotes are the weakest: one story is vivid but cannot prove a general claim.

teach.body: The warrant explains why the evidence supports the claim. Turnover fell at St. Anne's (evidence), so Pinecrest should copy it (claim), because losing experienced nurses is costly (warrant). Sometimes the warrant is stated, as in sentence 5; often it is left unstated and you must supply it. If the bridge is missing or shaky, even accurate evidence fails to support the claim.

teach.caption: Emotional appeal alone is not evidence: it moves the reader without proving the claim.

teach.h: Mapping an argument in four moves
items: Find the claim: the sentence that states what should be done or believed (often first or last).
Mark each reason (why) and the evidence under it (statistics, studies, experts, examples, anecdotes).
Spot signal words for the other side: 'some argue', 'critics say', 'opponents claim' (counterclaim).
Find the answer that follows, often after 'however' or 'but' (rebuttal).

teach.text: Common mix-ups: calling the counterclaim the author's own view (it is the view the author rejects), calling a restated claim 'evidence', and treating a vivid anecdote as strong proof. Judge an argument by its support, not by whether you agree with it.

teach.body: Brianna Scott, applying to a nursing program, maps the Pinecrest letter. She marks sentence 1 as the claim because it says what should be done. Sentence 3 is a statistic and sentence 4 an example, so both are evidence. Sentence 6 begins 'Some board members argue', the counterclaim; sentence 7 begins 'However' and answers it, the rebuttal. When asked about sentences 6 and 7, she picks 'They present and answer an objection.'

items: Claim = the position; reasons = why; evidence = proof.
Evidence types: statistics, research findings, expert testimony, examples, anecdotes.
The warrant explains why the evidence supports the claim.
Counterclaim = the other side; rebuttal = the author's answer to it.
Ethos, pathos, logos: an emotional appeal alone is not evidence.

summary: You can now take an argument apart into its claim, reasons, evidence, warrant, counterclaim and rebuttal. You can also name the type of evidence and the kind of appeal an author uses.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Many teens spend hours each day on their phones. (2) Some of that time is spent on schoolwork and staying in touch with family. (3) Still, our school should ban phones during class periods. (4) Teachers report losing several minutes of each lesson to phone distractions. (5) Schools that adopted bans have reported calmer classrooms.

Which sentence states the author's claim?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
A.why: Sentence 3 states the position the author argues for: the school should ban phones during class. Sentences 4 and 5 support it.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 is background that introduces the topic.
whyNot.1: Sentence 2 concedes a point to the other side before the claim.
whyNot.2: Sentence 4 is evidence (teacher reports) supporting the claim.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Our city should plant more street trees in the Eastside neighborhood. (2) Eastside has the fewest trees and the hottest summer sidewalks in the city. (3) Some residents worry that tree roots will crack the sidewalks. (4) But newer planting methods guide roots downward, away from the pavement.

What is the function of sentence 4?
options: It states the author's main claim.
It rebuts an objection to the claim.
It presents a reason for the claim.
It introduces a counterclaim.
A.why: Sentence 3 raises an objection (roots cracking sidewalks); sentence 4, signaled by 'But', answers that objection. That is a rebuttal.

whyNot.0: The claim is in sentence 1: plant more street trees.
whyNot.2: Sentence 2 gives the reason; sentence 4 responds to an objection instead.
whyNot.3: Sentence 3 is the counterclaim; sentence 4 answers it.

A.q: An article arguing that adults should get more sleep includes this sentence: 'Dr. Hannah Lee, director of the Midvale University sleep laboratory, says most adults she studies sleep less than they believe.' What type of evidence is this?
options: A statistic
An anecdote
Expert testimony
A personal example
A.why: The sentence reports the view of a qualified expert, named with her credentials. That is expert testimony.

whyNot.0: No number or percentage is given.
whyNot.1: An anecdote is a personal story; this is a qualified person's professional view.
whyNot.3: The writer gives no example from personal life.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Picture a seven-year-old standing alone at a dark bus stop at 6 a.m., shivering, because her parents have already left for the early shift. That is the reality for dozens of families in our district. The school board must start a before-school program now.

Which appeal does the author mainly use?
options: Ethos, by citing the author's own credentials
Logos, by presenting statistics and research
Pathos, by creating sympathy for a lone child
Logos, by comparing the costs of programs
B.why: The image of a shivering child alone in the dark is designed to stir feeling. That is an appeal to emotion (pathos).

whyNot.0: The author never mentions personal credentials or expertise.
whyNot.1: 'Dozens of families' is vague; no statistics or studies are given.
whyNot.3: No costs are mentioned or compared.

B.q:
Read the passage.

The county should require bike helmets for riders under 18. In a recent study at Riverbend Hospital, children treated for bike crashes who wore helmets were far less likely to suffer serious head injuries than those who did not.

Which statement best expresses the warrant that links the evidence to the claim?
options: Laws that require safety gear can reduce serious injuries.
Riverbend Hospital treats many children for bike crashes.
Most young riders in the county already wear helmets.
Teen riders are less careful than adults on bicycles.
B.why: The evidence shows helmets reduce head injuries; the claim is that a law should require them. The bridge is the assumption that requiring the gear will lead to fewer serious injuries.

whyNot.1: This is a detail about the study's setting, not the reasoning that connects study to law.
whyNot.2: If most already wore helmets, a law would matter less; this does not link the evidence to the claim.
whyNot.3: The argument never compares teen and adult riders.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Our clinic should switch to online appointment booking. (2) Online booking would let patients schedule at any hour. (3) Front-desk staff currently spend about three hours a day answering scheduling calls. (4) Online booking is the right choice for our clinic. (5) Two nearby clinics cut missed appointments after making the switch.

Which sentence restates the claim instead of supporting it?
options: Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 5
B.why: Sentence 4 repeats the claim from sentence 1 in different words. It adds no reason or evidence.

whyNot.0: Sentence 2 gives a reason: patients could book at any hour.
whyNot.1: Sentence 3 is evidence about staff time spent on calls.
whyNot.3: Sentence 5 is evidence from other clinics' results.

C.q:
Read the passage.

City Council should extend library hours to 9 p.m. on weeknights. Many students work after school and cannot reach the library before it closes at 6. Last year, a pilot program at the Oak Branch kept the doors open until 9 and saw evening visits climb every month.

Which sentence, if added, would serve as a rebuttal to a likely counterclaim?
options: Students use the library to study, print papers and use the internet.
The Oak Branch pilot ran for twelve months before it ended last fall.
Some council members have said longer hours would cost too much.
The added staff cost is less than one percent of the library budget.
C.why: A likely objection is cost. A sentence showing the cost is small answers that objection directly, which is what a rebuttal does.

whyNot.0: This adds a reason about library uses; it does not answer an objection.
whyNot.1: This adds detail about the pilot; it responds to no counterclaim.
whyNot.2: This states the counterclaim itself, not a rebuttal to it.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) As a school nurse for nineteen years, I have treated hundreds of students for dehydration. (2) Our school should install water bottle filling stations in every hallway. (3) Students who carry refillable bottles drink more water during the day, according to a state health department survey. (4) Some argue that the stations are too expensive. (5) Yet each station costs less than the school spends on bottled water in a single semester.

Which choice correctly matches a sentence to its role?
options: Sentence 1: logos, using a statistic
Sentence 3: research finding as evidence
Sentence 4: the author's main claim
Sentence 5: a counterclaim to the main claim
C.why: Sentence 3 cites a state health department survey, a research finding used as evidence for the claim in sentence 2.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 establishes the author's credibility (ethos); 'hundreds' is not a statistic used as logic.
whyNot.2: The claim is sentence 2; sentence 4 presents the opposing view.
whyNot.3: Sentence 5 answers the objection, so it is the rebuttal.

C.q:
Read the passage.

The Riverside Gazette should stop printing on Mondays. My neighbor Frank says he never reads the Monday paper, and neither do I. Printing costs keep rising, and the Monday edition is always the thinnest of the week.

Which part of the argument offers the weakest support for the claim?
options: The neighbor's remark about the Monday paper
The point that the cost of printing keeps rising
The point that the Monday edition is the thinnest
The author's statement that the paper should stop
C.why: One neighbor's habit plus the author's own is anecdotal evidence: too few readers to show anything about the paper's audience. The cost and size points at least bear on the whole edition.

whyNot.1: Rising costs are a relevant reason to cut an edition.
whyNot.2: A thin edition is relevant evidence that Monday offers little content.
whyNot.3: This is the claim itself, not support for it.

reteach.title: Think of a courtroom
reteach.question: In a trial, the lawyer states what she will prove, calls witnesses, shows exhibits, and answers the other side. How does a written argument match that?

blocks.body: The lawyer's opening statement is the claim. Each line of argument ('my client was at work') is a reason. Witnesses and exhibits are the evidence. The closing explanation of why the exhibits matter is the warrant. When the other side objects, that is the counterclaim, and the lawyer's answer is the rebuttal. A lawyer who simply repeats 'my client is innocent' louder has not added evidence.

blocks.text: The objection belongs to the other side. On the TEAS, a sentence that begins 'Critics argue' or 'Some say' is usually the counterclaim, not the author's view.

explain.body: The claim is the author's position: what the reader should believe or do. It is often signaled by should, must or needs to, and it usually appears near the start or the end.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hospital parking costs patients' families up to $20 a day. (2) Families of long-stay patients often visit daily for weeks. (3) Some families say they visit less because of the cost. (4) Hospitals should offer free parking passes to families of long-stay patients.

Which sentence is the claim?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
test.why: Sentence 4 states what should be done; sentences 1 to 3 give the facts and reasons that support it.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 is a supporting fact about cost.
whyNot.2: Sentence 2 is a supporting fact about how often families visit.
whyNot.3: Sentence 3 is supporting evidence about the effect of the cost.

explain.body: A reason says why the claim is right. Evidence proves the reason: statistics, research findings, expert testimony, examples or anecdotes. A sentence that only repeats the claim is neither.

test.q: An essay claims that schools should offer free breakfast to all students. Which sentence is EVIDENCE rather than a reason or the claim?
options: Every student deserves to start the day well fed.
Hungry students have a harder time focusing in class.
Free breakfast should be offered at every school.
After Lincoln Middle added it, tardiness fell 12%.
test.why: A specific result at a named school with a percentage is evidence. It proves that breakfast programs have measurable effects.

whyNot.0: This is a value statement offered as a reason, with no proof.
whyNot.1: This is a reason (why breakfast matters) without data to prove it.

explain.body: A counterclaim is the opposing view the author raises, often after 'some argue' or 'critics say'. The rebuttal is the author's answer, often after 'however', 'but' or 'yet'. Raising and answering an objection makes an argument stronger.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Our town should build a dog park. (2) Dog owners now crowd the soccer fields. (3) Critics say barking would disturb nearby homes. (4) Yet the proposed site is a quarter mile from the nearest house.

Which sentence is the counterclaim?
options: Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
test.why: Sentence 3, signaled by 'Critics say', presents the opposing view the author then answers.

whyNot.1: Sentence 4 answers the objection, so it is the rebuttal.
whyNot.3: Sentence 2 is a reason supporting the claim.

explain.body: Ethos builds trust in the speaker (credentials, experience). Pathos stirs emotion (vivid images, fear, sympathy). Logos uses logic and data. Pathos can persuade, but on its own it proves nothing.

test.q: A speaker urging flu shots says, 'I have been a pharmacist for twenty-two years, and I get my shot every fall.' Which appeal is this?
options: Pathos, because it frightens the listener
Logos, because it presents survey results
Ethos, because it builds trust in the speaker
Logos, because it compares the risks of the flu
test.why: Citing twenty-two years as a pharmacist builds trust in the speaker. That is an appeal to credibility (ethos).

whyNot.0: Nothing in the sentence is designed to frighten.
whyNot.1: No survey or data is presented.
